title: Life is short (here's how to spend it by ex-Snapchat CSO & Wall Street, Imran Khan)
guest: Imran Khan, founder and CIO of Prime Asset Management, host of 'Conference', former Chief Strategy Officer of Snapchat, ex-Wall Street banker and analyst
summary: Interview with Imran Khan, former Snapchat CSO and 15-year Wall Street veteran, covering compounding in money and relationships, how getting laid off as a bottom-quartile banking analyst became his career breakthrough, staying even-keeled, learning from young people, public speaking, and why he built his invite-only 'Conference' as a community. The hosts' takeaways connect his stories to Atomic Habits, their own 'wake up' moments of leaving the prescribed finance path, and the value of leaders who respect every job.

ideas.idea: Most people underestimate the power of compounding: start investing early, keep it conservative, and let time do the work rather than chasing lottery wins.
ideas.detail: Imran's advice to his 35-year-old self: a dollar growing 15% a year doubles in five years, quadruples in ten and becomes 16x in twenty, which builds substantial financial safety without doing anything fancy.

ideas.idea: Relationships compound too; aim for a few high-quality relationships that grow over time and add a few more each year.
ideas.detail: It is not about having many relationships but about strong roots across different areas by the time you get older; Imran also says true friends are texting-relationship friends, since email is impersonal and if someone won't pick up your call it is not a real relationship.

ideas.idea: Long hours in banking are mostly a sign of inefficiency, not of workload, so efficiency and focus matter more than hours.
ideas.detail: Imran worked 90-100 hour weeks as a telecom banking analyst in 2000; afterward 50-60 hour weeks felt like a massive upgrade, and he cites Wall Street Journal reporting on Bank of America health problems as evidence the industry still has not fixed its work process.

ideas.idea: Every job is hard, and leaders should respect every job rather than assuming their own is the hardest.
ideas.detail: Imran worked in a school library and a grocery store in college and says being a waiter is probably as tough as being a Wall Street analyst; the hosts add that this respect cascades down through culture when a leader believes it, and hypothesize it comes from leaders who have experienced hardship themselves.

ideas.idea: Failure can give you clarity: being a bad analyst and getting laid off pushed Imran into the small-shop equity research role that became his big career breakthrough.
ideas.detail: He was bottom quartile as a banking analyst (poor attention to detail, weak English writing, hated PowerPoint), was laid off in 2001 when the telecom bubble burst, and could only get a job at a tiny research shop, which he needed to keep his visa.

ideas.idea: Working 30 more hours a week than your peers compounds into an enormous knowledge edge within a year.
ideas.detail: Carrying a 100-hour banking work ethic into a 70-hour research job made Imran far more productive than colleagues, which is what freed him to take on extra coverage.

ideas.idea: At a small firm you can volunteer to cover what nobody else is covering; being a big fish in a small pond creates opportunities a big-name firm would never give you.
ideas.detail: Imran asked his boss to let him cover internet stocks in his free time and picked up Yahoo, Amazon and eBay at the bottom of the market; when they rallied he looked like a genius, JP Morgan and other big banks called, and he says at a big bank someone more qualified would already have covered those names.

ideas.idea: The skills that make a bad junior analyst can be irrelevant at the senior level, where banking becomes a relationship business.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: Imran later returned to banking as a managing director and head of group and did very well because, by MD level, the job depends on people liking you rather than on PowerPoint and attention to detail.

ideas.idea: Never get over-excited or over-depressed: when everyone is uber-hyped be nervous, and when everyone is depressed expect the day after tomorrow to be beautiful.
ideas.detail: Imran says this is his natural personality (his dad was hurt when a gift got only an 'OK' reaction); the hosts note that internally he was even-keeled but externally cheerful at Snapchat, and contrast it with lore about Jeff Weiner's early hot-headed reputation at LinkedIn.

ideas.idea: Being dismissive of young people is a career killer; as you age, who you learn from should flip from older people to people in their 20s and 30s.
ideas.detail: Older people's learning curves plateau while younger people take more risks and bring new experiences; Imran credits working with 20-somethings at Snapchat as the best thing about joining, and the hosts say this belief is what let him build his relationship with Evan Spiegel.

ideas.idea: For public speaking, read the audience and adjust in real time, and do not over-rehearse.
ideas.detail: Imran was a high school debater, makes eye contact to check whether the message resonates, refuses to see interview questions in advance because rehearsing makes him worse, and treats a talk to 2,000 people like a regular conversation.

ideas.idea: If people aren't engaging, find the relevancy that connects your topic to what they care about rather than pushing on.
ideas.detail: His example: he knows nothing about baseball and will zone out, so someone who wants to talk baseball should bring in cricket, which he grew up watching in Bangladesh, to get him engaged.

ideas.idea: It is OK to be 90% perfect when speaking; audiences are human and are rooting for you, not waiting for you to fail.
ideas.detail: Imran says who cares if a speech flops, that is what makes you human; Cherie adds a Stanford public speaking course's takeaway that listeners want you to succeed and recover when you stumble.

ideas.idea: Build a community of interesting, heterogeneous people rather than a conference of big names, and keep it small enough that people actually talk.
ideas.detail: Conference mixes founders, CEOs, regulators, lawyers, nonprofit leaders and young people to avoid group-think, grew from 50 to 100 to 160 attendees, and requires speakers to contribute four to six hours instead of 'speak and leave'; Imran says he doesn't need to watch Elon Musk on stage since his thoughts are on X in real time.

ideas.idea: A curated, hand-selected community makes people feel safe, so everyone attends sessions and genuinely wants to meet each other.
ideas.detail: Cherie noticed everyone at Conference sat through sessions and hung out at dinners and drinks because each person was a first-degree connection of Imran and trusted his curation.

ideas.idea: Small daily actions compound into big results, per Atomic Habits: habit-stack and never skip more than two or three days.
ideas.detail: The hosts extend compounding from finance to habits, citing the gym and Cherie's 2025 goal of eating 40 different fruits and vegetables a week, tracked on paper, and recommend James Clear's Atomic Habits.

ideas.idea: Being responsive to friends in small consistent ways is how relationships compound into a powerful network.
ideas.detail: Jean notes Imran manages hundreds of millions of dollars yet texts friends back within a minute about 90% of the time, and that consistent small acts of care are what made Conference possible.

ideas.idea: Failing at the prescribed path can be a 'wake up' moment that leads to a better-fitting career.
ideas.detail: Jean only looked at product management after failing to land PE or hedge fund roles out of Goldman Sachs fund-of-funds investing; she references Vu Tran's 'the path and waking up' idea and Graham Weaver's realization at a PE shop that a colleague loved the work in a way he never would.

ideas.idea: If the person next to you loves the work in a way you never will, they will excel in ways you can't, which is a signal to change paths.
ideas.detail: Jean's desk neighbor at Goldman traded volatility in every spare minute while she read fashion blogs, which showed her that finance was not her calling.

ideas.idea: Life can have many acts; reinvention is possible at almost any stage even if it gets harder with kids and mortgages.
ideas.detail: Jean says she is on her third act in her 30s and anticipates more, and the hosts speculate that midlife crises are wake-up moments where people feel it is too late to change.

ideas.idea: Write notes to your future self so that when you become a manager you remember to listen to the people below you.
ideas.detail: Jean received a 2013 email from herself via futureme.org reminding her that a manager had dismissed a feature idea of hers that turned out great, and to not do the same when she leads teams.

ideas.idea: Studying Gen Z and Gen Alpha now helps you anticipate how society will act over the next 10 to 30 years.
ideas.detail: Jean says she is obsessed with forming her own hypotheses about younger generations' driving needs and motivations because they will shape the future world.

ideas.idea: There is no strict pattern that childhood rule-breakers become the successful adults; Imran was a strict rule follower and still built an unconventional career.
ideas.detail: Imran followed rules growing up in Bangladesh to avoid corporal punishment at school and from a tough mother, and has never had a speeding ticket; the hosts note most guests claim to have been rule breakers.
